topic: Family Law: Hindu Law (Marriage, Succession, and Guardianship)
description: This module explores the codified personal laws governing Hindus (including Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs) in India. It covers the essential conditions for a valid marriage, grounds for divorce, the revolutionary changes in property succession rights, and the legal framework for the guardianship of minors.

hindu_marriage_act_1955.concept: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA): Conditions and Status
key_points: Conditions for Valid Marriage (Section 5): Neither party should have a living spouse (Monogamy); valid consent (sound mind); age (Groom 21, Bride 18); parties are not within 'degrees of prohibited relationship'; and parties are not 'Sapindas' of each other (unless custom permits).

Void Marriages (Section 11): A marriage is 'void ab initio' (invalid from the very beginning) if it violates the rules of monogamy, prohibited degrees, or sapinda relationship. It has no legal existence.

Voidable Marriages (Section 12): A marriage is valid until annulled by a competent court. Grounds include impotence, lack of valid consent (force or fraud), or the wife being pregnant by some other person at the time of marriage.

Divorce by Mutual Consent (Section 13B): Parties can jointly file for divorce if they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, have not been able to live together, and have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved. There is a mandatory 6-month 'cooling-off' period (which courts can sometimes waive).

hindu_succession_act_1956.concept: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (HSA) and the 2005 Amendment
key_points: Coparcenary Property (Mitakshara School): Refers to ancestral property where rights are acquired by birth. Historically, only male lineage (sons, grandsons, great-grandsons) were coparceners.

The Landmark 2005 Amendment: Section 6 was amended to grant daughters equal rights in the coparcenary property. A daughter of a coparcener now becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right, with the same rights and liabilities as a son, irrespective of her marital status.
Class I Heirs: When a Hindu male dies intestate (without a will), his property devolves simultaneously and equally upon his Class I heirs, which include his widow, mother, sons, and daughters.

Natural Guardians (Section 6): In the case of a boy or an unmarried girl, the natural guardian is the father, and 'after' him, the mother. (The Supreme Court in Githa Hariharan v. RBI clarified that 'after' means 'in the absence of', allowing the mother to act as guardian even if the father is alive but absent/negligent).
Custody of Tender Age: The custody of a minor who has not completed the age of five years shall ordinarily be with the mother.

Welfare Principle (Section 13): In the appointment or declaration of any person as guardian of a Hindu minor, the 'welfare of the minor' shall be the paramount consideration. No person can be appointed if the court believes it goes against the child's welfare.

mcq_bank.subtopic: Conditions of a Valid Hindu Marriage

questions.question: Under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, which of the following is an absolute essential condition for a valid Hindu marriage?

options.A: The bride and groom must belong to the same caste.
options.B: Neither party must have a spouse living at the time of the marriage (Monogamy).
options.C: The marriage must be registered within 30 days.

questions.explanation: Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act enforces strict monogamy. If either party has a living spouse at the time of marriage, the subsequent marriage is null and void under Section 11, and constitutes the crime of bigamy.

questions.question: Ramesh, a Hindu, dies without leaving a will in 2024. He leaves behind ancestral coparcenary property. He is survived by his wife, one son, and one married daughter. Who has the right to claim a share in his ancestral coparcenary property?

options.A: Only the son, as daughters lose their property rights upon marriage.
options.B: Only the son and the wife.
options.C: The son and the daughter have equal rights as coparceners by birth, regardless of the daughter's marital status.
options.D: The property automatically transfers to the State.

questions.explanation: Following the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, Section 6 was amended to make daughters (whether married or unmarried) coparceners by birth, granting them the exact same rights and liabilities in ancestral property as sons.

questions.question: Two first cousins (the children of two brothers) marry each other according to Hindu rites. There is no established custom in their community that permits such a marriage. Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, what is the legal status of this marriage?

options.A: It is a perfectly valid marriage because they consented.
options.B: It is a 'voidable' marriage, meaning it is valid until one of them files for annulment.
options.C: It is 'void ab initio' (invalid from the beginning) because they fall under the 'degrees of prohibited relationship' and 'sapinda relationship'.
options.D: It is valid but they will be fined by the family court.

questions.explanation: Under Section 5(iv) and (v) of the HMA, parties must not be sapindas or within the degrees of prohibited relationship (which includes first cousins). If they are, and no custom permits it, the marriage is strictly 'void' under Section 11, meaning it has no legal existence whatsoever.
